items.title: O'Connell v DPP; DPP v O'Connell [2026] HCA 41 — appeal courts must allow for the jury's advantages
items.citation: [2026] HCA 41 (Gageler CJ, Gordon, Edelman, Steward, Gleeson, Jagot and Beech-Jones JJ, 4 November 2026)
items.significance: The ACT Court of Appeal overturned a jury's murder verdict as unreasonable and entered manslaughter; a unanimous High Court said it failed to allow fully for the jury's advantages and sent the case back.
core_labels: The role of juries, including verdicts
items.document: Cases/Crime/O'Connell v DPP; DPP v O'Connell [2026] HCA 41 - Case Summary.pdf
items.document11: Cases/Year 11/Year 11 - O'Connell v DPP; DPP v O'Connell [2026] HCA 41 - Case Summary.pdf
items.lead:
In April 2022 **Michael O'Connell** drove off with Ms Jordan on the bonnet of his car; she fell and died. In a
circumstantial case, a **jury convicted him of murder** (reckless indifference to the probability of death); he was
sentenced to 15 years. In 2025 the **ACT Court of Appeal** (2–1, McCallum CJ dissenting) held the verdict
**unreasonable** and entered **manslaughter** (10 years). Both sides appealed.
items.use_it_for:
- **crime.4.5 (appeals)** — every layer of appeal at work, and the limits on appeal judges second-guessing a jury.
- **crime.3.9 (juries)** — respect for the jury's advantages in seeing the evidence.
items.caution:
A **class case summary**; the file's paragraph numbers appear one too high, so quotes are cited to the reasons only.
Edelman J's point about probability was not a ground of appeal.

sections.Three courts, three answers:
| | Jury (2023) | ACT Court of Appeal (2025) | High Court (4 November 2026) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Verdict | Murder | Murder set aside; **manslaughter** entered, 2–1 | DPP appeal allowed **unanimously**; orders set aside |
| Reasoning | — | Jury's advantages could not resolve its doubt; speed critical | Majority failed to make full allowance for the jury's advantages (*M v The Queen*), and decided on a hypothesis not raised at trial |
| Substitution | — | Entered the lesser verdict the jury rejected | O'Connell's appeal on s 37O dismissed |
| Result | 15 years | 10 years | **Remitted**: the Court of Appeal must decide the unreasonable-verdict ground again |

items.title: R v Sharma [2026] NSWDC 402 — act proven but not criminally responsible: the mental health impairment defence
items.citation: [2026] NSWDC 402 (Noman SC DCJ, judge alone, 4 November 2026)
items.significance: A man who wounded his wife was found 'act proven but not criminally responsible' because a delusional disorder stopped him reasoning about wrongfulness — detention and Tribunal review, not a sentence.
core_labels: The elements of crime: actus reus, mens rea
items.document: Cases/Crime/R v Sharma [2026] NSWDC 402 - Case Summary.pdf
items.document11: Cases/Year 11/Year 11 - R v Sharma [2026] NSWDC 402 - Case Summary.pdf
items.lead:
**Rajendra Sharma** was charged with **wounding his wife with intent to murder** (alternatively intent to cause grievous
bodily harm) and breaching an AVO, after an assault on 23 June 2024. A delusional fixation about her fidelity had
developed from 2021. Crown and defence agreed the **mental health impairment** defence was established, and the
matter was heard by a judge alone.
items.use_it_for:
- **crime.3.8 (defences)** — a complete defence that turns on mens rea and capacity, proved by the accused on the
  balance of probabilities.
- **crime.1.2** — why criminal responsibility needs a guilty mind.
- **Balance** — community protection and the victim's interests through detention and Tribunal oversight rather than
  punishment.
items.caution:
A **class case summary**. A special verdict is **not a conviction**; the diagnosis is unsettled. The victim and son are not
named. Family violence context: teach with care.

sections.Held:
- On two psychiatrists' evidence, Noman SC DCJ was satisfied **on the balance of probabilities** that a delusional
  disorder meant Mr Sharma **could not reason about whether his act was wrong** (s 28).
- **Special verdict** (s 31): "**act proven but not criminally responsible**" — covering the AVO breach too.
- **Orders**: detention (ss 33–34) and referral to the **Mental Health Review Tribunal**, which decides release. The
  victim's statement was received.

items.title: WA serial child sex offender freed under a 41-condition supervision order (ABC, 4 November 2026)
items.citation: Evidence summary of Jake Sturmer, ABC News, 4 November 2026, reporting Solomon J's decision in the Supreme Court of WA under the High Risk Serious Offenders Act 2020 (WA); Fardon v Attorney-General (Qld) [2004] HCA 46; Garlett v Western Australia [2022] HCA 30
items.significance: The court found Dennis McKenna a high risk serious offender but chose 41 supervision conditions over indefinite detention — post-sentence orders weighing community protection against liberty.
items.document: Crime/Media/Crime - McKenna High Risk Offender Supervision Order Evidence Summary.pdf
items.lead:
**Dennis McKenna** has served **15.5 years** in prison since 2011 for child sex offences. The State applied for a
restriction order; on 4 November 2026 Justice Solomon found him a **high risk serious offender** but made a
**supervision order** with **41 conditions** (including no contact with his 29 victims, per the ABC) rather than a
continuing detention order. Release is expected within weeks.
items.use_it_for:
- **crime.4.8 (post-sentencing)** — preventive orders, supervision and the end of a sentence.
- **Balance and rights** — detention for what a person might do, not what they have done.
items.caution:
A **class evidence summary of a news report**; the judgment was not located. Earlier reports counted 28 victims; the
ABC's 29 is unexplained.

sections.Continuing detention v supervision (WA,:
| | Continuing detention order | Supervision order (McKenna) |
|---|---|---|
| Where | Stays in custody after the sentence ends | Released under conditions |
| Duration | Indefinite, until rescinded (s 26) | For the period stated (s 27) |
| Test | State proves an unacceptable risk to a high degree | Court must be satisfied supervision adequately manages the risk |
| Paramount | **Community protection** | Community protection |

*Fardon* (2004) upheld post-sentence preventive detention; *Garlett* (2022) upheld WA's scheme. Victims' interests enter
only through conditions.

items.title: Darwin teenager charged with terrorism and 3D-gun blueprint offences (ABC, 29 October 2026)
items.citation: Evidence summary of an ABC News report, 29 October 2026, and the NT Joint Counter Terrorism Team statement; Criminal Code Act 1995 (Cth) ss 101.5, 474.45C, 474.45H; Crimes Act 1914 (Cth) ss 15AA, 20C
items.significance: A child faces adult Commonwealth terrorism charges, including a 2026 offence for 3D-printed gun blueprints — federal counter-terrorism law meeting youth justice in bail, identity and sentencing.
items.document: Crime/Media/Crime - NT Teen Terrorism Charge and Youth Bail Evidence Summary.pdf
items.document11: Preliminary/Year 11 - Experiences with the Law - NT Teen Terror Charges Evidence Summary.pdf
items.lead:
After a Crime Stoppers tip-off about violent extremist material online, the NT Joint Counter Terrorism Team
executed warrants in Darwin on **28 October 2026** and charged an unnamed teenager with three Commonwealth
offences: **s 101.5** (collecting or making documents likely to facilitate terrorism, max 10 or 15 years) and two
online-material offences, including **s 474.45C** aimed at 3D-printed firearm blueprints (max 5 years each).
Police said there was no information the teen could access or make a firearm. He was remanded; bail is listed
for **9 November 2026**. **All matters are allegations; he is presumed innocent.**

  modified.

sections.Children v adults charged with terrorism:
| | Adult | Child |
|---|---|---|
| Offences and maximums | Same | Same — no lower federal ceiling |
| Court | Adult courts exercising federal jurisdiction | Youth court; s 20C lets it treat the charge as a territory offence |
| Bail | s 15AA presumption against bail: exceptional circumstances | Same test; community protection paramount, child's best interests primary |
| Bail appealed | Prosecution notice stays the grant | Same — the Law Council says it should not apply to children |
| Sentencing | s 19AG limits discretion | Age, maturity and family weighed; the Law Council wants an s 19AG exemption |

items.title: Gavin v Greenstone Financial Services Pty Ltd [2026] NSWCATAD 339 — interim reinstatement refused
items.citation: [2026] NSWCATAD 339 (Dr L Kirk, Senior Member, 4 November 2026)
items.significance: A probationary employee with endometriosis asked NCAT to reinstate her while her disability discrimination complaint is investigated; the Tribunal applied injunction principles and refused.
core_labels: The role of courts and tribunals
items.document: Cases/Human Rights/Gavin v Greenstone Financial Services Pty Ltd [2026] NSWCATAD 339 - Case Summary.pdf
items.document11: Cases/Year 11/Year 11 - Gavin v Greenstone Financial Services Pty Ltd [2026] NSWCATAD 339 - Case Summary.pdf
items.lead:
Ms Gavin began as a claims agent on **13 April 2026** with six months' probation. During a performance improvement plan
she disclosed **endometriosis** and asked for adjustments (19 August); the employer decided to terminate (4 September).
She complained to **Anti-Discrimination NSW** and asked NCAT for **interim orders** reinstating her. She appeared for
herself; the employer had counsel.
items.use_it_for:
- **hr.2.11 / hr.2.9** — how state anti-discrimination law is enforced: complaint to Anti-Discrimination NSW, then NCAT.
- **Access to justice** — a self-represented worker against a represented employer; interim relief is hard to win.
items.caution: A **class case summary of a procedural ruling only**. The employer's submissions mis-cite two sections.

sections.Held — application dismissed (17 Septemb:
- The s 105 interim power is guided by the principles for an **interlocutory injunction**: a **prima facie case** and the
  **balance of convenience**.
- No prima facie case on the evidence, and the balance favoured the employer.
- The **complaint itself is undecided**.

items.title: Reddit and the Digital Freedom Project take the under-16s social media ban to the High Court (The Guardian, 3 November 2026)
items.citation: Evidence summary of Josh Taylor, The Guardian Australia, 3 November 2026, on Reddit, Inc v Commonwealth (S166/2025) and Digital Freedom Project Incorporated v Commonwealth (S163/2025), heard 3 and 4 November 2026; read with Part 4A of the Online Safety Act 2021 (Cth) and eSafety's March 2026 survey
items.significance: Reddit and a libertarian group ask the High Court to strike down the under-16s social media ban, testing whether an implied freedom, not a bill of rights, can check a law protecting children.
core_labels: A contemporary issue illustrating the promotion and/or enforcement of human rights
items.document: Human Rights/HR - Reddit v under-16s ban (High Court) - hearing Evidence Summary.pdf
items.document11: Preliminary/Year 11 - Reddit v under-16s ban (High Court) Evidence Summary.pdf
items.lead: The first major legal challenge to the under-16s social media ban was heard in the High Court on **3 and 4 November 2026**. Australia has no guaranteed right to free speech, so both challengers rely on the **implied freedom of political communication**: they say stopping under-16s holding accounts burdens political communication, and the Commonwealth says the law serves a legitimate purpose, reducing harm from features such as algorithms, infinite scroll and notifications. **No decision has been made.**
items.use_it_for:
- **hr.2.8 The role of the Constitution**: no bill of rights, an implied freedom made by judges, and a court asked to weigh a new community value (child safety online) against it. Fits HSC 2024 Q22 (the Constitution and changing values); the summary's exemplar paragraph answers it.
- **hr.3.1 A contemporary issue**, with hr.2.11 (courts) and hr.2.9 (statute law); also compliance, as eSafety investigates five platforms.
items.caution: A preview of an **undecided case**, not a judgment: update this record when the Court rules. The parties' submissions could not be opened, so their arguments are as reported. Read from a saved copy of the Guardian article. The tests come from secondary summaries; check the High Court's reasons before quoting them.

sections.The two challenges:
| | Reddit | Digital Freedom Project (led by NSW Libertarian MP John Ruddick) |
|---|---|---|
| Argument | Platforms are a common source of political information; teens could not post, comment or react on politics | Adopts much the same argument on the burden on political communication |
| Hurdle | Whether the burden is justified | The Commonwealth says the group has **no standing**: it has not identified any activity of its own that is impeded. Its two teenage plaintiffs withdrew in July |
sections.How the court decides: An implied-freedom case asks, in turn: is there a burden on political communication; is the law's purpose legitimate; is it suitable, necessary and adequate in balance (the structured proportionality test from *McCloy v NSW* (2015)). Commentators are divided: Prof Anne Twomey saw a possible mismatch between purpose and effect; Prof Luke Beck expected the challenges to fail.
sections.The numbers, checked:
- **Ten** platforms had to restrict under-16 accounts from **10 December 2025**. The Prime Minister says more than **5 million** accounts were suspended; eSafety reported about **4.7 million** by mid-December 2025. These count accounts, not children.
- eSafety's March 2026 survey found the share of under-16s holding an account fell from **52.4% to 42.1%**: a modest but real fall, and evidence for both sides on whether the ban works.
- The maximum penalty was doubled from **$49.5 million to $99 million** by an Act assented to on 11 September 2026; the Guardian's "nearly $100m" is consistent.
- The government says the **digital duty of care** bill would "require the same action"; the bill is s…

All seven justices heard the joined special case; state and territory attorneys-general intervened for the
Commonwealth.

| Whose freedom | Serious for a group without the vote | The freedom protects electors' communication |
| Purpose | Accept protecting young people is legitimate | Protects children from engagement-driven features |
| Effectiveness | Under-16s evade age checks; content still viewable logged out | Rules are consultative, targeted, adjustable |

items.title: NT and Queensland shut a UN expert out of youth detention (Amnesty International, 2 November 2026)
items.citation: Evidence summaries of an Amnesty International Australia media release, 2 November 2026, and Chloe Chomicki, ABC News, 4 November 2026, on the refusal of the UN Special Rapporteur on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples' requests to visit Holtze (NT) and Cleveland (Qld) youth detention centres; UNDRIP; OPCAT (ratified December 2017); CROC arts 37(b), 40(1)
items.significance: A UN expert invited to Australia was refused entry to two youth detention centres holding mostly First Nations children — the third UN access dispute since 2022.
core_labels: The role of the United Nations
items.document: Human Rights/HR - UN rapporteur refused detention access - ABC report Evidence Summary.pdf
items.lead:
The Special Rapporteur's official visit runs **2–13 November 2026**. The NT and Queensland refused planned visits to
**Holtze** and **Cleveland**, where about **97%** of children at Cleveland were Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander at
inspection. It is the second time in under a year the NT has blocked UN experts. First Nations young people are detained at **25.7 per 10,000** (2024–25), against a
Closing the Gap target of a 30% fall by 2031; the Productivity Commission assesses no change.
items.use_it_for:
- **hr.2.2 / hr.2.1** — UN monitoring inside a sovereign, federal state; the Commonwealth answers internationally for
  detention run by states and territories.
- **Year 11 (the global legal system)** — state sovereignty and the UN's role.
items.caution: A **class evidence summary of an NGO advocacy release**; no government explanation is included.

sections.What the mandate asks v what happened:
| UN terms of reference | November 2026 |
|---|---|
| Access to all places of detention | Holtze and Cleveland visits refused |
| Confidential contact with detainees | No in-centre contact with children |
| Contact with authorities in every branch | NT and Qld refused to engage, the Rapporteur says |
| Freedom of movement | Visit otherwise proceeding |
| Findings reported to the Human Rights Council | Precedent: the WGAD relied on public reports for the NT |

The terms of reference are UN guidelines, not a treaty: visits depend on the state's invitation and cooperation.
sections.ABC report (4 November 2026):
Queensland gave a brief statement; the NT and the Commonwealth did not respond. Cleveland held **101** children against a
safe capacity of **95** (August 2025); about **90%** at Cleveland identified as Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander (68.2%
across Queensland's centres). First Nations young people are detained at **26 times** the non-Indigenous rate (2023–24).
Queensland's mandatory 12 months for serious offending on bail starts on 30 November. Special Rapporteurs visit under UN
terms of reference, **not OPCAT**; cooperation rests on invitation. Preliminary findings are due in Sydney on **13
November 2026**.
sections.Use it for:
- **hr.2.2 / hr.2.1** — UN monitoring inside a sovereign, federal state; the Commonwealth answers internationally for
  detention run by states and territories.
- **Year 11 (the global legal system)** — state sovereignty and the UN's role.

items.title: DV Commissioner warns online misogyny is outpacing the law (ABC, 5 November 2026)
items.citation: Evidence summary of Claudia Long, ABC News, 5 November 2026, interviewing Micaela Cronin, Domestic, Family and Sexual Violence Commissioner; National Plan to End Violence against Women and Children 2022–2032 and its Second Action Plan; Online Safety Act 2021 (Cth) and the Digital Duty of Care Bill 2026
items.significance: Harmful attitudes form online years before any offence: the Commissioner calls for funded prevention, a digital duty of care and action on overdue recommendations — the limits of reactive DV law.
items.document: Family/Evidence Summaries/Family - DV Commissioner Manosphere Warning Evidence Summary.pdf
items.lead:
Commissioner **Micaela Cronin** says online misogyny ("the manosphere") is shaping young men's attitudes faster than
law and policy can respond. In one survey **24.7%** of boys aged 13–17 agreed feminism may be violently resisted; **70%**
of 2,600+ teachers saw manosphere ideas affect students in the past year; reported sexual violence rose **64%** over 15
years. Of 21 Rapid Review recommendations (August 2024), responses have been "progressive".
items.use_it_for:
- **fam.2.4** — the effectiveness of legal and non-legal responses to DV; prevention versus punishment.
- **fam.2.6** — statutory and non-government bodies driving reform.
items.caution:
A **class evidence summary of a report built around one official's views**; some study figures and wording in the article
do not match the originals (the 24.7% is boys 13–17, not "Gen Z men").

sections.Legal v non-legal responses:
| | Legal | Non-legal |
|---|---|---|
| Timing | Mostly after harm; coercive control (s 54D) from 1 July 2024 | Prevention and early intervention target attitudes first |
| Online | Digital duty of care Bill (passed the House 28 October) | Respectful relationships education; 95% of teachers say some students need it |
| Oversight | Courts, police | The Commission monitors the National Plan; Second Action Plan from 2027 |
sections.Use it for:

- **fam.2.6** — statutory and non-government bodies driving reform.

items.title: Daphne & Nirmal [2026] FedCFamC2F 58 — family violence, unacceptable risk and graduated time
items.significance: The court found a father committed family violence and that unsupervised time was an unacceptable risk — even though his intimidation conviction and AVO had been overturned on appeal.
items.document11: Cases/Year 11/Year 11 - Daphne & Nirmal [2026] FedCFamC2F 58 - Case Summary.pdf
items.lead:
Two parents sought final parenting orders for children aged **10 and 8**. In 2023 the father was found guilty of
intimidation and a two-year AVO protected the mother, but in early 2025 the **District Court quashed the conviction and
dismissed the AVO**. The trial ran over four days in September 2025.
items.use_it_for:
- **fam.2.2 / fam.2.4** — best interests and safety under the 2024 parenting provisions; family violence findings in
  family law.
- **Civil v criminal standard** — the same conduct, different outcomes in different courts.
items.caution:
A **class case summary**; sensitive (family violence, children). The independent children's lawyer is named
inconsistently, and the catchwords and reasons cite different sections.

sections.Held — Judge Suthers:
- The father was a **perpetrator of family violence** (including controlling behaviour at a doorway incident) — the
  family court decides on the **balance of probabilities**, so a quashed criminal conviction does not decide the issue.
- Unsupervised time posed an **unacceptable risk** to the children.
- **Orders (38 parts):** children live with the mother, who has **sole parental responsibility**; time with the father
  begins **supervised** and graduates, with safe changeovers; a neutral expert explains the orders to the children,
  whose wish to see their father is respected.
- The judge criticised **both** parents for escalating the conflict.
sections.Use it for:
- **fam.2.2 / fam.2.4** — best interests and safety under the 2024 parenting provisions; family violence findings in
  family law.
- **Civil v criminal standard** — the same conduct, different outcomes in different courts.
sections.Caution:
A **class case summary**; sensitive (family violence, children). The independent children's lawyer is named
inconsistently, and the catchwords and reasons cite different sections.

items.title: Rahman & Rahman (No 3) [2026] FedCFamC2F 1203 — no full and frank disclosure, no property order
items.significance: A husband sought 55% of a 40-year marriage's property but repeatedly failed to disclose his overseas companies and accounts — so the court dismissed his application.
items.document11: Cases/Year 11/Year 11 - Rahman & Rahman (No 3) [2026] FedCFamC2F 1203 - Case Summary.pdf
items.lead:
The parties married in 1986 and emigrated in 1992. The husband filed for property orders in February 2025 seeking **55%**
of the net property; the wife had dropped her own claim. After interim orders (a $50,000 partial settlement and a
disclosure deadline) he missed the trial date, filed his affidavit and financial statement late, and made an unsuccessful
recusal application.
items.use_it_for:
- **fam.2.3** — the steps in a property settlement and why disclosure is the foundation.
- **Year 11 (civil law)** — the burden of proof in civil proceedings.
items.caution:
A **class case summary** (pseudonyms). One paragraph of the judgment is corrupted, and hearing dates differ between the
header and the reasons.

sections.Held — application dismissed:
- The husband breached his duty of **full and frank disclosure**: his overseas company interests and bank accounts were
  never identified or valued.
- Without that, the court could not find it **just and equitable** to alter property interests; the husband bore the
  **onus** and had not shown the facts for the orders he sought. The wife held nearly all the known assets.
- Costs were reserved.
sections.Use it for:
- **fam.2.3** — the steps in a property settlement and why disclosure is the foundation.
- **Year 11 (civil law)** — the burden of proof in civil proceedings.
sections.Caution:
A **class case summary** (pseudonyms). One paragraph of the judgment is corrupted, and hearing dates differ between the
header and the reasons.

items.title: Rogge and Loos (Child support) [2026] ARTA 2605 — no calendars, so the Tribunal splits the difference
items.citation: [2026] ARTA 2605 (General Member S Hoffman, Perth, 25 August 2026)
items.significance: Two self-represented parents disputed how many nights their daughter spent with each; with no records, the Tribunal set aside a 75/25 decision and fixed care at 70/30.
core_labels: The roles of courts and dispute resolution methods
items.document: Cases/Family/Rogge and Loos (Child support) [2026] ARTA 2605 - Case Summary.pdf
items.document11: Cases/Year 11/Year 11 - Rogge and Loos (Child support) [2026] ARTA 2605 - Case Summary.pdf
items.lead:
A 2016 parenting plan recorded care of a girl (born 2012) as **65% mother, 35% father**. In 2024 the mother told Child
Support that care had changed from 14 August 2022; on objection, Child Support decided **75/25**. The father sought
review. Both parents were self-represented; the hearing was by video with an interpreter.
items.use_it_for:
- **fam.2.2** — care percentages drive child support; small changes in nights change who pays.
- **fam.2.5 / tribunals** — informal, accessible review for self-represented parents, and its limits when evidence is
  missing.
items.caution:
A **class case summary** of a single-member decision (pseudonyms). The decision has no paragraph numbers, and the
night arithmetic and the mother's 2024 overseas claim are loosely reasoned.

sections.Held — decision set aside:
- Neither parent had kept a calendar. The Tribunal accepted the father had not provided all the care the plan expected,
  but could not fix the exact nights.
- It **split the difference**: 254 nights to the mother, 111 to the father — **70/30** from 14 August 2022, with the old
  65/35 revoked as of 13 August 2022.
sections.Use it for:
- **fam.2.2** — care percentages drive child support; small changes in nights change who pays.
- **fam.2.5 / tribunals** — informal, accessible review for self-represented parents, and its limits when evidence is

items.title: Statham & Statham [2026] FedCFamC2F 182 — property settlement after a husband's bankruptcy
items.significance: The husband's only asset — shares giving a right to live in the family apartment — had vested in his bankruptcy trustee, yet the court divided the property and gave the shares to the wife.
items.document11: Cases/Year 11/Year 11 - Statham & Statham [2026] FedCFamC2F 182 - Case Summary.pdf
items.lead:
In 2015–16 the husband bought company shares, secured by a loan, that carried the **right to occupy an apartment** where
the wife and children lived; from 2021 the wife paid the loan. In early 2023 the husband became **bankrupt** and the
shares vested in his **trustee**; the bank sued for possession. The wife sought property orders, and days before the
hearing the husband's agent registered a **charge** on the shares.
items.use_it_for:
- **fam.2.3** — property orders under s 79 and the Family Law Act's power to bind a bankruptcy trustee (s 90AE).
- **Contributions** — financial contributions (loan payments) and housing for the children.
items.caution:
A **class case summary** (pseudonyms). Marriage length and separation date are muddled in the judgment; coercive control
allegations were not determined; some statutory extracts are not verbatim.

sections.Held — Judge Colquhoun:
- It was **just and equitable** to alter property interests even though the main asset had vested in the trustee.
- Using a **two-pool** approach, the wife's contributions to the shares were assessed at **100%**: the shares were
  **transferred to her** and she takes over the loan.
- The court could not order the non-party agent to remove the charge, so it ordered the **husband** to remove it. His
  adjournment request was refused.
sections.Use it for:
- **fam.2.3** — property orders under s 79 and the Family Law Act's power to bind a bankruptcy trustee (s 90AE).
- **Contributions** — financial contributions (loan payments) and housing for the children.
sections.Caution:
A **class case summary** (pseudonyms). Marriage length and separation date are muddled in the judgment; coercive control
allegations were not determined; some statutory extracts are not verbatim.

items.title: Peak body pitches a 7.5% short-stay levy to fund NSW social housing (ABC, 4 November 2026)
items.citation: Evidence summary of Declan Bowring, ABC News, 4 November 2026, on CHIA NSW's commissioned research (McKell Institute land tax modelling); Short Stay Levy Act 2024 (Vic); State Environmental Planning Policy (Housing) 2021 (NSW)
items.significance: With 72,000 households on the waitlist, CHIA NSW proposes a 7.5% levy on short stays, as Victoria has, to raise $135m a year — a peak body driving law reform through new taxes.
items.document: Shelter/Evidence Sheets/Shelter - Short Stay Levy for Community Housing Evidence Summary.pdf
items.lead:
The **Community Housing Industry Association NSW** (CEO Luke Achterstraat) presented research at NSW Parliament on 4
November 2026: a **7.5%** short-stay levy could raise about **$135m a year**, and its broader options (mostly land tax)
about **$26bn** over 10 years. NSW's $6.6bn Building Homes for NSW program promises 8,400 public homes.
items.use_it_for:
- **shel.3.4** — funding social and community housing; a hypothecated tax versus planning caps.
- **Law reform** — a non-government stakeholder proposing a new law.
items.caution:
A **class evidence summary of an advocacy proposal**; the revenue figures are CHIA NSW and McKell modelling, not
independently verified, and the report was not obtained.

sections.Victoria v NSW:
| | Victoria (levy) | NSW (planning controls) |
|---|---|---|
| Law | *Short Stay Levy Act 2024*, from 1 January 2025 | SEPP (Housing) 2021, framework from 1 November 2021 |
| Mechanism | **7.5%** of booking fees for stays under 28 days, earmarked for housing | Mandatory register, code of conduct; 180-day cap on non-hosted stays in some areas |
| Who pays | Booking platform, or the owner for direct bookings | Host registers; $65 first-year fee |
| Housing revenue | Yes | None |

The Government, Opposition, Greens and industry responded; NSW announced a short-term rental review in December 2023.
sections.Use it for:
- **shel.3.4** — funding social and community housing; a hypothecated tax versus planning caps.
- **Law reform** — a non-government stakeholder proposing a new law.

items.title: Priced out of parenthood — Sydney house prices and falling births (SMH, 5 November 2026)
items.citation: Evidence summary of Matt Wade and Bronte Gossling, The Sydney Morning Herald, 5 November 2026, reporting unpublished KPMG analysis (Terry Rawnsley); ABS Births 2024
items.significance: Sydney neighbourhoods with median house prices of $400k–$900k fell from 199 to 86 in five years, and births hit a 20-year low — unaffordable shelter shaping whether people start families.
items.document: Shelter/Evidence Sheets/Shelter - Priced Out of Parenthood Sydney House Prices and Births Evidence Summary.pdf
items.lead:
KPMG compared house prices and births across Greater Sydney neighbourhoods in 2019 and 2024. Neighbourhoods with median
prices of **$400k–$900k** fell from **199 to 86**; Greater Sydney had **58,122** births in 2024, a reported 20-year low.
Sydney's fertility rate (**1.4**) compares with **1.98** in NSW outside Sydney (ABS gives NSW overall as 1.46). The
Sydney median house price is **$1.66m** (September quarter 2026), 7.9% below its peak. One family moved to Newcastle to
afford a home.
items.use_it_for:
- **shel.1.4 / shel.1.3** — affordability and its social consequences; whether planning, tax and lending laws are doing
  enough, fast enough.
items.caution:
A **class evidence summary of a news report of unpublished consultancy analysis**; neighbourhood and regional fertility
figures were not independently checked. No government response.

sections.The legal levers (not discussed in the a:
Planning (the Housing SEPP's low- and mid-rise reforms), stamp duty concessions for first home buyers, the
Commonwealth 5% Deposit Scheme and the National Housing Accord.

items.title: Tiny homes for homeless people stalled by caravan-era planning rules (ABC, 4 November 2026)
items.citation: Evidence summary of Brooke Chandler, ABC Illawarra, 4 November 2026; Local Government (Manufactured Home Estates, Caravan Parks, Camping Grounds and Moveable Dwellings) Regulation 2021 (NSW) cl 77; Local Government Act 1993 (NSW) s 68; Wingecarribee LEP 2010 cl 5.5
items.significance: A charity's plan to put tiny homes for homeless people on private rural land stalls because clause 77 lets a moveable dwelling be lived in long term only by the owner's household or disaster victims.
items.document: Shelter/Evidence Sheets/Shelter - Lydias Legacy Tiny Homes Planning Rules Evidence Summary.pdf
items.lead:
About **72** people are homeless each night in the Southern Highlands; priority social housing waits are about 5 years
and average waits over 10 (Argyle Housing). Southern Highlands charity **Lydia's Legacy** wants to place moveable tiny
homes (8 m by 2.5 m, up to **$150,000** each) on private rural land offered by a landowner.
items.use_it_for:
- **shel.3.2 / shel.2.8** — planning law, not tenancy law, deciding whether shelter is provided at all; law reform lagging
  a housing crisis.
items.caution: A **class evidence summary of a local feature**, sympathetic to the charity; figures are service-provider estimates.

sections.Granny flat v tiny home on wheels:
| | Granny flat (secondary dwelling) | Tiny home on wheels (moveable dwelling) |
|---|---|---|
| Legal category | A dwelling under the planning instruments and LEP | A caravan, if registrable as a trailer |
| Approval | Development application; fast-track CDC unavailable in rural zones | No approval if the **cl 77** exemption applies; otherwise DA and s 68 |
| Who may live there | Can be rented once approved | Long term only by the **owner's household** or disaster victims — not a homeless tenant |

A 2026 Legislative Council inquiry reported in March; the government supported **3 of 6** relevant recommendations in
principle.
sections.Use it for:
- **shel.3.2 / shel.2.8** — planning law, not tenancy law, deciding whether shelter is provided at all; law reform lagging
  a housing crisis.
sections.Caution: A **class evidence summary of a local feature**, sympathetic to the charity; figures are service-provider estimates.

items.title: Coalition urges a $1bn homelessness prevention push — Right Help, Right Time (4 November 2026)
items.citation: Evidence summary of a Medianet media release, 4 November 2026, launching the Right Help, Right Time campaign and open letter at NSW Parliament (Uniting NSW.ACT, NCOSS, Mission Australia, Homelessness NSW, Domestic Violence NSW, Youth Action and others), checked against AIHW, Street Count and DCJ data
items.significance: Eleven NGOs frame homelessness as a failure of early help and seek $1bn over four years; most of their figures check out, but the claim that it would save $2.1bn is unsupported.
core_labels: The roles of courts and tribunals
items.document: Shelter/Evidence Sheets/Shelter - Right Help Right Time Early Intervention Release Evidence Summary.pdf
items.use_it_for:
- **shel.3.2 / shel.2.6** — NGOs and the media as drivers of law and policy reform on homelessness; prevention versus
  crisis response.
- **Evaluating sources** — an advocacy release whose claims can be checked against official data.
items.caution:
A **class evidence summary of a sector campaign release** with no cited sources and no government response. The source
link is the NSW Street Count release used to check the figures.

sections.Claims v official data:
| Coalition claim | Official or primary data |
|---|---|
| Nearly 700,000 in NSW at risk of homelessness | Impact Economics model: **696,442** (2022) — a model, not a headcount |
| Almost two in three seeking emergency housing don't get it | AIHW 2024–25: **35%** of clients needing it were provided it |
| Rough sleeping up 75% in five years | Street Count: **1,319** (2020) → **2,308** (2026) |
| Priority waitlist doubled | **5,800** (June 2021) → **12,478** (March 2026) |
| Rents up 48% | Median $460 → $680, 2020–25 (DCJ, via Homelessness NSW) |
| $1bn over four years avoids up to $2.1bn in costs | **No costing published** |

The 2021 Census counted 35,011 people homeless in NSW. Several fig…
sections.Updated summary (5 November):
The campaign's open letter to **Premier Chris Minns** proposes a **Preventing Harm Framework**, shifting spending from crisis
to early intervention. Spokespeople included Ben Keneally (Uniting), Dom Rowe (Homelessness NSW) and Delia Donovan (DV NSW).
**59 people a day** were turned away from NSW homelessness services in 2024–25. The 75% rough-sleeping rise and the
12,478 waitlist are Homelessness NSW analyses of government data.
